questions.stem: English ‘tree’, French ‘arbre’ and German ‘Baum’ all refer to the same thing. This best shows that the link between a word and its meaning is:
options: decided by whichever sounds are easiest for speakers to say
arbitrary, but fixed by the conventions of each speech community
iconic, because each word imitates a feature of the thing it names
set by a grammar that is shared by every human language
questions.explanation: Three unrelated forms name the same referent, so nothing in the sounds themselves links them to the meaning; each community simply agrees on its own word. If words were iconic, the three would resemble one another and the tree.

questions.stem: Words such as ‘sizzle’, ‘buzz’ and ‘hiss’ are often given as partial exceptions to the arbitrariness of language because:
options: they are bound morphemes that cannot stand alone
their meanings are identical in every language
they have connotations but no denotation at all
their sounds imitate the sounds they refer to
questions.explanation: Onomatopoeic words echo the sounds they name, so the link between form and meaning is not wholly arbitrary. They are only partial exceptions, though: a dog says ‘woof’ in English but ‘wang wang’ in Mandarin, so even these words follow each language's conventions.

questions.stem: A speaker says, ‘Bone the buried dog the.’ Every word is a real English word, but the utterance breaks the conventions of which subsystem?
questions.explanation: Syntax is the set of conventions for ordering words into phrases, clauses and sentences, and English requires an order like ‘The dog buried the bone.’ Each word is morphologically well formed, so the fault is not in morphology.

questions.stem: In one Year 11 friendship group, ‘crisp’ comes to mean ‘excellent’ (‘That goal was crisp’), and soon everyone in the group understands it. This shows that:
options: a new meaning exists only once a dictionary has recorded it
slang has none of the conventions that govern Standard English
meaning is arbitrary, but becomes shared once a group adopts it
a word's meaning is fixed by its etymology and cannot really change
questions.explanation: Nothing about the sounds of ‘crisp’ means ‘excellent’; the group agrees on the new sense, and that shared convention makes it meaningful. Dictionaries record meanings after communities create them, so the meaning was real before any dictionary noticed it.

questions.stem: ‘The 86 tram leaves Bourke Street every ten minutes.’ Which function of language does this utterance mainly serve?
questions.explanation: The referential function conveys information about the world, here a timetable fact. The phatic function builds social connection rather than passing on content.

questions.stem: Passing a colleague in a corridor, Sam says, ‘Hey, how’s it going?’ and keeps walking. Which function does this utterance mainly serve?
questions.explanation: The phatic function establishes or maintains social contact; Sam does not expect a real account of the colleague's day. Although it is a question, it is not seeking information, so it is not mainly referential.

questions.stem: In class, a student asks, ‘Is “irregardless” actually a word?’ Which function of language does this utterance mainly serve?
questions.explanation: The metalinguistic function uses language to talk about language itself, here the status of a word. The utterance does ask for information, but what it is about is language, which makes it metalinguistic rather than referential.

questions.stem: Which utterance mainly serves the conative function?
questions.explanation: The conative function engages the addressee to get them to do something, and this request does exactly that. The statement about the salt is referential, the exclamation is emotive and the greeting is phatic.

questions.stem: The SunSmart slogan ‘Slip! Slop! Slap!’ is a set of commands, but its alliteration and rhythm also give it which other function of language?
questions.explanation: The poetic function draws attention to the form of the message itself, through patterning such as alliteration and rhythm, which also makes the slogan memorable. The commands are conative, but the sound patterning is what gives it the poetic function.

questions.stem: A teacher, wanting a student to shut the window, says, ‘Is anyone else cold in here?’ Which function does the utterance mainly serve?
options: metalinguistic, because it is a question
conative, although its form is interrogative
referential, because it asks for information
phatic, because it starts a conversation
questions.explanation: Function depends on intent in context, not on sentence type: the teacher's aim is to get a student to act, which is conative. Taking it as referential misses that no one is expected simply to report on their temperature.

questions.stem: Ava tells her friend about a holiday she took in Broome two years ago. Which property of human language does this most clearly show?
questions.explanation: Displacement is the ability to talk about things removed in time and space from the moment of speaking. Productivity is about creating new utterances, which is not the point of this example.

questions.stem: Speakers can produce and understand sentences they have never met before, such as ‘The purple wombat recited the tax code.’ This property of human language is called:
questions.explanation: Productivity (or creativity) is the capacity to combine a finite set of units into an unlimited number of new, meaningful utterances. Displacement concerns talking about things not present, which is not what makes this sentence possible.

questions.stem: The same small set of sounds, none meaningful on its own, can be recombined to form ‘pat’, ‘tap’ and ‘apt’. This property, in which meaningless units combine into meaningful ones, is:
questions.explanation: Duality of patterning means language is organised on two levels: meaningless sounds, and the meaningful words built from them. Semanticity is simply the fact that signals carry meaning, not the two-level structure.

questions.stem: A baby born in Melbourne to Vietnamese-speaking parents is adopted by an English-speaking family and grows up speaking only English. This shows that language is acquired through:
options: cultural transmission rather than genetic inheritance
genetic inheritance passed on from the child's birth parents
displacement, since the parents were not present
duality of patterning, which links sounds to meaning
questions.explanation: Humans learn the particular language of the community they grow up in; the language is passed on culturally, not in the genes. The child's birth parents' language did not appear, which rules out genetic inheritance.

questions.stem: Vervet monkeys have distinct alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, but cannot combine them to signal ‘an eagle was here yesterday’. Which two properties of human language do the calls lack?
questions.explanation: The calls cannot be combined into new messages (productivity) or refer to a past event (displacement). They do carry meaning, are separate signals that any vervet can give and bear no resemblance to the predator, so the other properties are present.

questions.stem: In the study of situational context, tenor refers to:
options: the relationship between participants, including social distance
the subject matter or topic that a text deals with
whether the text is delivered in spoken, written or signed form
the time and place in which the text occurs
questions.explanation: Tenor concerns who the participants are to each other: their social distance and the formality this calls for. The subject matter is the field, and the time and place make up the setting.

questions.stem: In a match report, words such as ‘handball’, ‘mark’ and ‘behind’ mainly reflect the text's:
questions.explanation: Field is the subject matter, and these lexemes belong to the field of Australian football. Tenor would show in the formality and the relationship with the reader, not in the topic vocabulary.

questions.stem: A doctor tells a colleague, ‘The patient presented with an acute myocardial infarction’, then tells the patient's son, ‘Your dad’s had a heart attack.’ The doctor is mainly adjusting:
options: mode, because only the second utterance is spoken
dialect, to signal a different regional identity
register, to suit a different tenor and audience
field, because the subject matter has changed
questions.explanation: The topic stays the same; the doctor shifts from technical jargon to everyday lexis because the son is a non-specialist with a different relationship to the doctor. Both utterances are spoken, so mode has not changed.

questions.stem: Register differs from dialect and sociolect because register is language variation defined by:
options: the historical period in which a text appears
use: the situation, purpose and relationship
user: the speaker's region or social group
the speaker's age, gender and social class
questions.explanation: Register varies with use, so one speaker shifts register across situations. Dialects and sociolects vary with the user, identifying where speakers come from or which social group they belong to.

questions.stem: Two written messages: ‘Dear Ms Nguyen, I am writing to request an extension for my History essay.’ and ‘hey can u ask nguyen 4 an extension on the history essay?’ The main factor behind the difference is:
options: mode: one message is spoken and the other written
text type: only one of them is a written text
tenor: the social distance between the participants
field: the messages deal with different subject matter
questions.explanation: Both messages share a field (an essay extension) and a mode (writing); what differs is the relationship with the reader, a principal versus a friend. Greater social distance brings formal address, full spelling and standard punctuation.

questions.stem: A eulogy is written in advance and then delivered aloud. Compared with spontaneous conversation, it would be expected to contain:
options: fewer non-fluency features, such as false starts and filled pauses
more overlapping speech and minimal responses from the audience
more ellipsis and unfinished clauses, as in casual conversation
fewer prosodic features, such as stress, pitch and intonation
questions.explanation: A prepared text has been planned and often rehearsed, so hesitations, false starts and repairs are far less frequent. It is still spoken, so prosody stays fully present and is often used deliberately for emphasis.

questions.stem: A family says a grandparent has ‘passed away’ rather than ‘died’ when telling a young child. This choice is influenced most by:
options: mode: the conventions that apply to written language
setting: the time of day the conversation takes place
cultural context: shared values and taboos around death
field: the technical vocabulary of medicine and health
questions.explanation: Euphemism for death reflects the values, attitudes and beliefs of the wider community, which is cultural context. The conversation is spoken and everyday, so neither medical field nor written conventions explain it.

questions.stem: A council notice reads: ‘Residents are reminded that bins must be placed kerbside by 6 am.’ The agentless passive ‘are reminded’ most likely serves the writer's purpose by:
options: signalling that the notice is a spontaneous text
showing that the information in it is uncertain
putting residents in front position while keeping the council impersonal
making the notice sound more casual, personal and friendly in its tone
questions.explanation: The passive makes ‘residents’ the subject and omits the agent, so the council's authority is implied without being stated. This raises formality and social distance, the opposite of a casual tone.

questions.stem: Describing someone as ‘slender’ rather than ‘skinny’ mainly changes the word's:
options: connotation, while the denotation stays largely the same
denotation, while the connotation stays largely the same
word class, from an adjective to an adverb
morphology, by adding a derivational affix
questions.explanation: Both words denote being thin, but ‘slender’ carries positive associations and ‘skinny’ often negative ones. The choice shows that language is not a neutral window on the world.

questions.stem: How many morphemes does ‘unhappiness’ contain?
questions.explanation: It contains the prefix un-, the free root happy and the suffix -ness. The y-to-i spelling change does not add a morpheme.

questions.stem: Which word contains a derivational suffix?
questions.explanation: The suffix -ness derives a new word and changes the class from adjective to noun. The -ed, -s and -est suffixes are inflectional: they mark tense, number and degree without creating a new lexeme.

questions.stem: The -ing in ‘The players were running’ is inflectional, but the -ing in ‘The building is old’ is derivational. What makes the second one derivational?
options: inflectional suffixes can attach only to nouns
derivational suffixes always follow a free root
it turns a verb into a noun, creating a new lexeme
it marks the progressive aspect of the verb build
questions.explanation: In ‘building’ the suffix creates a noun with its own meaning, so it is derivational. In ‘running’ the word stays a form of the verb ‘run’, with -ing marking progressive aspect, which is inflectional.

questions.stem: In ‘The cat sat on the mat’, which words are function words?
questions.explanation: Function words such as determiners and prepositions carry grammatical relationships rather than much lexical meaning. Nouns and lexical verbs such as ‘cat’ and ‘sat’ are content words.

questions.stem: In ‘She can swim quickly’, the word ‘can’ is:
questions.explanation: ‘Can’ is a modal auxiliary expressing ability, and it supports the lexical verb ‘swim’. It is not the main verb, because ‘swim’ carries the core meaning of the verb phrase.

questions.stem: ‘Kick the bucket’, meaning ‘die’, is best described as:
options: a blend of parts of two separate words
an idiom, a type of multi-word lexeme
a compound formed from two free morphemes
a phrasal verb made of a verb and a particle
questions.explanation: An idiom is a multi-word lexeme whose meaning cannot be worked out from its parts, so it is stored as one unit. A phrasal verb combines a verb with a particle, as in ‘switch off’, which is not the structure here.

questions.stem: ‘Although it rained, we went to the beach and we swam.’ Which sentence structure is this?
questions.explanation: Two main clauses are coordinated by ‘and’, and a subordinate clause is introduced by ‘although’. Having both coordination and subordination makes it compound-complex, not merely complex.

questions.stem: In ‘The tall girl in the red hat laughed’, the noun phrase functioning as the subject is:
options: The tall girl in the red hat
questions.explanation: The whole noun phrase, with ‘girl’ as its head, pre-modified by ‘the tall’ and post-modified by the prepositional phrase ‘in the red hat’, is the subject of ‘laughed’. ‘The tall girl’ leaves out the post-modifier, which is part of the same phrase.

questions.stem: In ‘The committee elected Sam captain’, the word ‘captain’ functions as:
questions.explanation: ‘Captain’ completes the meaning by describing the object, ‘Sam’, after the verb, so it is an object complement. ‘Sam’ is the direct object, the one who was elected.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains an agentless passive?
questions.explanation: ‘Mistakes were made’ is passive and omits who made them, which can hide responsibility. The version with ‘by the minister’ is passive but names the agent, and the other two are active.

questions.stem: ‘Rose’, ‘tulip’ and ‘daisy’ are all ___ of ‘flower’.
questions.explanation: A hyponym is a more specific term included in a broader one, so each flower name is a hyponym of ‘flower’. ‘Flower’ is the hypernym, the umbrella term.

questions.stem: ‘I’ll meet you at the bank’ could refer to a riverbank or a financial institution. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The ambiguity comes from one word form with two unrelated meanings, which makes it lexical. Syntactic ambiguity arises from structure, as in ‘visiting relatives can be boring’, where the words themselves are not ambiguous.

questions.stem: Pitch, stress, volume, tempo and intonation are all:
questions.explanation: Prosodic features are the patterns of sound that run across speech, such as pitch and stress. Non-fluency features are things like filled pauses and false starts.

questions.stem: In speech, ‘I didn’t say SHE took it’, with heavy stress on ‘she’, implies that:
options: she borrowed rather than took it
I wrote it rather than said it
questions.explanation: Stress places the focus on one element and invites a contrast with alternatives, so stressing ‘she’ suggests another person took it. To imply borrowing, the stress would fall on ‘took’.

questions.stem: Said with rising intonation, ‘You’re coming?’ most likely functions as:
options: a command, because it is directed at the listener
a phatic greeting with no request for information
a statement, because its structure is declarative
a question, although its structure is declarative
questions.explanation: Prosody can override sentence structure: the rising intonation turns a declarative into a question asking for confirmation. Treating it as a plain statement ignores what the intonation adds.

questions.stem: In a transcript, a speaker's laughter, a whispered aside and a shrug are all examples of:
questions.explanation: Paralinguistic features are vocal effects and non-verbal communication that accompany speech. Discourse markers are words such as ‘well’ and ‘anyway’ that organise talk.

questions.stem: Which feature is typical of spontaneous speech but rare in edited writing?
options: false starts and filled pauses such as ‘um’
dense noun phrases built with nominalisation
questions.explanation: Spontaneous speech is produced in real time, so speakers hesitate, restart and repair. Edited writing removes these, and it relies on formatting and standard spelling, which speech does not have.

questions.stem: Written texts make up for the absence of prosody and paralinguistic features mainly through:
options: gesture, facial expression and eye contact
questions.explanation: Writers signal emphasis, tone and questions with punctuation, italics, capitals and careful word choice. Overlap and backchannels belong to conversation, which is exactly what writing lacks.

questions.stem: A: ‘How was the exam?’ B: ‘Don’t ask.’ B never says how the exam went, yet A understands it went badly. A's understanding comes mainly from:
options: inference from context and shared knowledge
the denotation of the words ‘don’t’ and ‘ask’
the syntax of a negative imperative sentence
the cohesive tie of anaphoric reference
questions.explanation: The literal meaning is an instruction not to ask, but A infers from context that the topic is unpleasant, which is the study of discourse and pragmatics. The denotations alone say nothing about the exam.
